papers.title: Coherence limitations of a Fourier-engineered $\cos(2\varphi)$ transmon qubit
papers.abstract: Intrinsically protected superconducting qubits are a promising route toward enhancing coherence times and advancing hardware towards applications in quantum computing. The $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit achieves protection against qubit relaxation by allowing only the coherent tunneling of pairs of Cooper pairs, resulting in Cooper-pair parity symmetry and thereby suppressing charge-induced errors. In this work, we experimentally realize a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit by Fourier engineering the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction superconducting circuit. Using an interference-based architecture, we are able to suppress the odd harmonics of an effective qubit potential and we observe good agreement between the measured transition spectrum and the effective theoretical model. We further investigate the energy relaxation time as a function of external flux and find that the qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point is limited by $1/f$ flux noise. This strong sensitivity arises from residual fluctuations in the first harmonic, which possesses a large prefactor despite being nominally canceled. In contrast, a fluxonium qubit with a similar energy spectrum and noise amplitude is less affected by flux noise, highlighting a key challenge for interference-based protection schemes.

summary.summary: This work experimentally realizes a $\cos(2\varphi)$ superconducting qubit using Fourier engineering of the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction circuit, achieving suppression of odd harmonics through an interference-based SQUID architecture. Despite the design's intended protection against charge noise, the qubit's lifetime at the flux symmetry point is strongly limited by $1/f$ flux noise due to residual first-harmonic fluctuations, reaching only $\sim 5$ µs compared to $\sim 130$ µs predicted for a fluxonium with matched spectrum.
summary.motivation: Intrinsically protected qubits offer a complementary approach to quantum error correction for reducing decoherence in superconducting circuits. The $\cos(2\varphi)$ potential realizes Cooper-pair parity protection to suppress charge-noise-induced relaxation, but the practical coherence limitations of interference-based implementations remain unexplored.
summary.method: A tunable multi-junction device with a fixed left arm (two junctions in series) and a tunable right arm (single junction plus small SQUID loop) was fabricated with $E_C/h = 0.21$ GHz and junction energies $E_{J,1}/h = 42.49$ GHz, $E_{J,2}/h = 53.9$ GHz, $E_{J,3}/h = 88.11$ GHz. Spectroscopy and time-domain measurements characterized the transition spectrum and energy relaxation as a function of flux bias, with noise contributions modeled using Fermi's golden rule.
summary.result: The qubit achieves a double-well potential consistent with theory, but $T_1$ at the symmetry point drops sharply to $\sim 5$ µs, dominated by $1/f$ flux noise ($A_{1/f} = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ Φ$_0$) coupling through residual first-harmonic terms with large prefactors. The same noise amplitude reduces a comparable fluxonium qubit's $T_1$ by only a factor of $\sim 5$, highlighting flux sensitivity as a fundamental challenge for this interference-based protection scheme.

papers.title: Revisiting the multi-mode rhombus circuit as a biased-noise qubit
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the idea of using an interferometer of pairs of Josephson junctions as a protected rhombus qubit. Unlike in the original proposal, where the qubit states are encoded into odd and even parity charge states, here, we intentionally alter the energy of one of the junctions to investigate the soft version of the rhombus qubit. This approach allows us to directly probe the qubit transitions over several GHz and reduce the potential drawbacks of the interferometer-based protection. Away from a half flux quantum external field, the large shunting capacitors of the circuit ensure localized qubit states in different phase valleys, leading to a biased-noise qubit. In the realized circuit, we measure an average $T_1\approx500\,μ$s relaxation time in the biased-noise regime (with a Ramsey dephasing time of $T^{R}_\varphi\approx90\,$ns), while an average $T_1\approx27\,μ$s relaxation time at frustration (with $T^{R}_\varphi\approx670\,$ns). Our loss analysis on this multi-mode circuit indicates that at low frequencies, flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling limit the relaxation times, pointing toward the presence of an optimal operating regime of around a few GHz.

summary.summary: This work revisits the rhombus qubit—a four-junction interferometer protected against charge noise—by intentionally introducing junction asymmetry ($\alpha = 0.63$) to raise the qubit frequency toward 100 MHz and mitigate low-frequency noise sources. The modified soft-rhombus qubit achieves $T_1 \approx 500$ μs in the biased-noise regime (away from frustration) and $T_1 \approx 27$ μs at half-flux frustration, with flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling identified as dominant loss mechanisms at low frequencies.
summary.motivation: While the symmetric rhombus provides protection against dielectric relaxation through charge-parity symmetry, its low transition frequency exposes it to 1/$f$ flux noise and quasiparticle-induced loss, motivating investigation of how circuit modifications can shift the optimal operating regime toward higher frequencies where these noise sources are suppressed.
summary.method: A soft-rhombus qubit was fabricated on sapphire with tantalum/aluminum-oxide junctions, where one junction has $E_J^{(4)} = 0.63 E_J$ relative to the other three. Circuit quantization, numerical simulations of multi-mode wavefunctions, and comprehensive noise analysis using Fermi's golden rule modeled relaxation from capacitive loss, drive-line coupling, flux noise ($A_\Phi = 4$ μΦ₀), and quasiparticle tunneling ($x_{qp} = 10^{-8}$).
summary.result: Ramsey dephasing times of $T_\varphi^R \approx 90$ ns in the biased-noise regime and $\approx 670$ ns at frustration agree with flux-noise models; relaxation measurements show that introducing asymmetry reduces coupling to $\sin(\hat{\phi}_i)$ operators and shifts the performance bottleneck to several GHz, where capacitive and Purcell losses dominate over low-frequency flux and quasiparticle noise.

papers.title: Surface-Code Thresholds and Qubit Footprints in Shuttling-Based Spin-Qubit Railways
papers.abstract: We present a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a $2\times N$ silicon spin-qubit railway architecture, utilizing electron shuttling to resolve the wiring fan-out bottleneck. Employing circuit-level noise modeling, we evaluate threshold performances across various noise biases. We demonstrate that shuttling check qubits instead of data qubits fundamentally improves system thresholds. Crucially, under a noise model biased towards dephasing for spin-qubit shuttling, the non-CSS XZZX surface code outperforms standard CSS variants. By tailoring the topological code to this specific inherent bias, we show that the Megaquop footprint is achievable with a distance 7 code requiring a $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, highlighting a pathway for substantial hardware reductions in early fault-tolerant quantum processors.

summary.summary: This paper develops a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a $2\times N$ silicon spin-qubit railway using coherent electron shuttling, with circuit-level noise modeling showing that the XZZX surface code outperforms CSS variants under dephasing-biased noise inherent to shuttling. A distance-7 code achieving Megaquop requires only $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, reducing qubit footprint by up to 72% compared to symmetric noise models.
summary.motivation: Silicon spin-qubit arrays face a wiring fan-out bottleneck in 2D layouts; shuttling-based 1D railway architectures offer a practical solution but require tailored error-correction strategies that account for the specific noise biases arising from micromagnet gradients and spin-orbit coupling during transport.
summary.method: The authors derive an asymmetric Pauli-channel noise model from the underlying Hamiltonian incorporating trajectory fluctuations through micromagnet fields and spin-orbit coupling effects, implement a unidirectional 'train schedule' syndrome extraction protocol satisfying stabilizer commutation, and compare XZZX versus CSS codes under check versus data shuttling using STIM circuit-level simulations with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding.
summary.result: Check-qubit shuttling with the XZZX code under $Z$-biased shuttling noise ($\eta = 100$, $\eta_Z = 100$) achieves a threshold of $p_\mathrm{th} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}$, substantially higher than CSS alternatives; at $p = 10^{-3}$ and full bias, distance-7 XZZX requires only 97 qubits (49 data, 48 check) for Megaquop, down from 1799 qubits in symmetric noise—a 72% footprint reduction.

papers.title: Syndrome resampling enhances quantum error correction thresholds
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) enables fault-tolerant quantum computation but requires operating quantum hardware at physical error rates below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. We introduce syndrome resampling, a general method that increases QEC thresholds of any decoder and suppresses logical errors without additional hardware, decoding modifications, or code-specific assumptions beyond syndrome statistics. The method exploits the fact that syndromes with low probability are likely to lead to logical failure, therefore biasing syndrome averages towards most likely syndromes effectively increases logical fidelities. We establish a direct connection between the Rényi coherent information (RCI) and powers of the syndrome probability distribution, showing that resampling syndromes according to these powers combined with maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) realizes a family of optimal thresholds associated with phase transitions in the RCI. Numerical simulations of surface codes demonstrate that syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders and reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in experimentally relevant regimes. We further show that syndrome resampling can be effectively implemented from finite data and combined with decoding-based post-selection to achieve additional gains. Finally, applying the method to existing experimental QEC data yields up to two orders of magnitude reduction in logical error rates without requiring additional measurements. Our results provide a practical and decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments.

summary.summary: Syndrome resampling (SR) enhances quantum error correction thresholds by reweighting syndromes according to powers of their probability distribution, establishing a connection to Rényi coherent information phase transitions. Applied to surface codes, SR reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in simulation and two orders in experimental lattice-surgery data without additional hardware or decoder modifications.
summary.motivation: Current superconducting qubit and trapped-ion QEC experiments operate near or above physical error thresholds, necessitating decoder-agnostic methods to suppress logical errors using only syndrome statistics.
summary.method: SR constructs the syndrome probability distribution $P(s)$ and resamples syndromes according to $Q_\alpha(s) = P^\alpha(s) / \sum_s P^\alpha(s)$, combined with maximum likelihood or minimum-weight perfect matching decoding. The method maps to phase transitions in the Rényi coherent information $I^{(\alpha)} = S^{(\alpha)}(\rho_Q) - S^{(\alpha)}(\rho_{RQ})$, generating a family of thresholds parametrized by $\alpha \geq 1$.
summary.result: For the $d=5$ surface code under bit-flip noise, MLD with SR achieves thresholds of $p_{\mathrm{th}} = 10.75(2)\%$ ($\alpha=1$), $17.74(3)\%$ ($\alpha=2$), and $20.93(2)\%$ ($\alpha=3$), compared to the standard $10.93\%$. On a superconducting-qubit lattice-surgery experiment with surface-17 code, SR applied to 44268 samples retains 40% while achieving logical error reduction comparable to post-selection ($5\%$ retention), yielding $\sim 100\times$ suppression of logical error rates.
